unit.title: Conversation Lab
unit.summary: Practice real-world pickleball conversations: game recaps, line calls, gear talk, watching together, ratings, fandom, invitations and say-this lines.

lessons.title: After her league night
lessons.objective: Respond with curiosity to a play recap without offering unasked-for advice.

payload.title: After league night
payload.setting: Alex texts after open play and mentions a tough match.

exchanges.theirMessage: Rough night. My dinking game was totally off.

replies.text: What went wrong with the dinks? Were they hitting the net or popping up?
replies.theirResponse: Both! Couldn't keep them low. Then they'd smash it.
replies.coachNote: Asking specifics shows you know the concept and care about details.

replies.text: That sounds frustrating. Dinking rallies are tricky.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, it's harder than it looks.
replies.coachNote: Honest sympathy is fine, but follow up with a question next time.

replies.text: Just hit harder next time.
replies.theirResponse: That's the opposite of what I should do.
replies.coachNote: Hard hits are the enemy of dinking. Don't advise unsolicited.

exchanges.theirMessage: If I could just keep them lower and in the kitchen...

replies.text: So lower = harder for them to attack. That makes sense?
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. A low dink is a good dink.
replies.coachNote: Restating what you heard earns trust and keeps the flow going.

replies.text: You'll get it next time.
replies.theirResponse: Hope so. Practice needed.
replies.coachNote: Generic encouragement is OK but doesn't deepen the talk.

replies.text: Dinking is boring anyway.
replies.theirResponse: ...It's literally the game.
replies.coachNote: Never dismiss the core strategy of the sport.

payload.closingNote: Dinking is a soft, low rally near the kitchen. Good dinking is the foundation of strong play.

statement.speaker: Casey
statement.text: We got pickled in that second game. I was so mad.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Her team lost 11-0, a shutout.
She is upset about one bad point.
They were actually winning but she's being humble.
She's confused about the score.

payload.translation: Pickled means losing a game 11-0 (shut out). It's one of the hardest losses to take.

followUps.line: Pickled is worse than a regular loss. That explains why she's frustrated.
Ask what happened that led to the blowout.
followUps.why: Natural follow-up to show you care about the story.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Shutout games hurt. Show empathy; don't minimize it or offer unsolicited fixes.

payload.prompt: After someone tells you about a rough game, which question is best?

options.text: What's one thing that went wrong, and what do you think you'll work on?
You should have played more aggressively.
Did you lose on purpose to make them feel better?
It's not a big deal, honestly.

explanation.correct: Open-ended questions about what went wrong and what's next show you care and you're listening.
explanation.incorrect: Follow-up questions should be curious and supportive, not dismissive or prescriptive.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask about what went wrong, then what she'll work on. That's real support.

pairs.definition: A soft, short shot that lands in the opponent's kitchen near the net.
The 7-foot no-volley zone on each side of the net.

explanation.summary: Dink = soft kitchen shot; pickled = shutout loss; kitchen = no-volley zone.
explanation.sayThisLine: Dinking in the kitchen is core pickleball. Pickled is rough.

lessons.title: The line call story
lessons.objective: Listen to a line-call dispute without taking sides or escalating.

payload.title: The line call story
payload.setting: Jordan is still steamed about a disputed call at open play.

exchanges.theirMessage: They called it out but I SAW it clip the line. I know what I saw.

replies.text: How did you handle it in the moment? Did you say something?
replies.theirResponse: I said I thought it was in, they didn't budge. So I let it go.
replies.coachNote: Asking how they handled it is neutral and shows you trust their judgment.

replies.text: Are you sure it was actually on the line?
replies.theirResponse: Yes. I was right there.
replies.coachNote: Doubting their account sounds like you don't believe them.

replies.text: They cheated you. That's unfair.
replies.theirResponse: I don't know if they cheated... it's just a bad call.
replies.coachNote: Don't assume bad intent in open play. It could be a genuine disagreement.

exchanges.theirMessage: It was at 9-9 too. Changed the whole game.

replies.text: Tight score like that and one call can swing it. Did you come back?
replies.theirResponse: We did, won the next point. But it stuck with me.
replies.coachNote: Acknowledging the impact and asking about recovery shows you understand stakes.

replies.text: That's rough.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, still bothering me.
replies.coachNote: Safe but doesn't keep the conversation going.

replies.text: Report them to the league. Get them banned.
replies.theirResponse: There's no league ref. It's open play.
replies.coachNote: Open play has no referees. Don't escalate friendly games.

payload.closingNote: In self-officiated play, line calls are sometimes contested. Listening without judgment is the best response.

statement.speaker: Quinn
statement.text: Everyone's calling lines so tight today. Half the balls on the line are going out.

payload.question: What is Quinn talking about?

options.text: Players are being stricter with line calls than usual; balls touching the line count as out.
The court's lines are faded, so calls are hard to make.
A new rule says lines don't count as in anymore.
The referees are favoring one side.

payload.translation: Players are making very strict calls today. In pickleball, lines are in, but some groups call them out more often than usual.

followUps.line: Strict calls are frustrating. That's a real thing that changes the game's feel.
followUps.why: Shows you understand the impact on play.

followUps.line: Ask if she's getting the benefit of the doubt or if it's both sides.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Line calls are subjective. Tight calls frustrate players. Listen without taking sides.

payload.prompt: When someone complains about a line call, the best response is to:

options.text: Ask how they handled it and show empathy for the frustration.
Tell them they should always appeal to the ref.
Insist that the other player must have cheated.
Say 'it's just a game' and move on.

explanation.correct: Listening and empathizing without assigning blame keeps the relationship strong.
explanation.incorrect: Escalating, dismissing, or assuming cheating doesn't help.
explanation.sayThisLine: Listen, empathize, ask how they handled it. That's support.

payload.prompt: In open play, if a ball touches the line, it is out. True?

scene.alt: Disputed line call at open play.

explanation.correct: In pickleball, lines are in. Any part of the ball touching a line is in.
explanation.incorrect: The official rule is that lines are in, always.
explanation.sayThisLine: When in doubt, the line is in. That's the rule.

lessons.title: The new paddle
lessons.objective: Ask smart gear questions without pretending expertise.

payload.title: The new paddle
payload.setting: Morgan just bought a new paddle and is excited about it.

exchanges.theirMessage: Picked up a carbon face paddle today. The spin on it is crazy.

replies.text: Is the spin making it harder or easier to control? How's it feel?
replies.theirResponse: Easier to control actually. More grip on the ball.
replies.coachNote: Asking about the feel and control shows real curiosity about the gear.

replies.text: Nice! That sounds expensive.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, but I wanted to try it.
replies.coachNote: Generic reaction. Ask about performance instead.

replies.text: Paddle doesn't matter that much. Skill is everything.
replies.theirResponse: It actually makes a difference. You'd feel it.
replies.coachNote: Gear matters. Don't minimize what she's excited about.

exchanges.theirMessage: I'm a little worried about the spin test coming soon, though.

replies.text: Will your paddle pass the test? Is that a real worry?
replies.theirResponse: Should be fine, but who knows. Hope so.
replies.coachNote: You named her concern directly and asked about it.

replies.text: I'm sure it will be fine.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, probably.
replies.coachNote: Reassurance is OK but asking about the issue is better.

replies.text: If it fails, that means it was cheating equipment.
replies.theirResponse: It's not cheating if it was approved before.
replies.coachNote: Don't call approved gear 'cheating.' That's insulting.

payload.closingNote: Paddle gear is a real part of the conversation. Ask about feel, control, and concerns without pretending expertise.

statement.speaker: Blake
statement.text: My new paddle is so gritty. I can put spin on dinks now that I never could before.

payload.question: What does Blake mean?

options.text: The paddle face is textured (rough/gritty), which creates more grip on the ball and more spin.
The paddle is dirty and Blake needs to clean it.
The paddle is low quality and falling apart.
The paddle is too hard and hurts Blake's arm.

payload.translation: A rough or textured paddle face grips the ball better, letting players create more spin. Smooth faces create less spin.

followUps.line: Rougher paddles = more spin. That's why spin tests matter now.
followUps.why: Shows you understand the connection to regulations.

followUps.line: Ask if Blake worries the texture is too rough for the new test.
followUps.why: Smart follow-up on the current gear discussion.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Paddle surface texture is real gear talk. Listen and ask; don't pretend to know materials science.

payload.prompt: When someone talks about a new paddle, what's the best question?

options.text: How does it feel? Is it easier to control or hit harder?
Is that the most expensive paddle on the market?
You should have gotten the other brand instead.
Paddle choice is totally personal, nobody agrees anyway.

explanation.correct: Asking about feel and control shows genuine interest in how the gear affects their play.
explanation.incorrect: Generic reactions, dismissing, or prescribing don't engage with what matters to them.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask about feel and control. That's gear talk.

payload.prompt: Which paddle face creates more spin?

image.alt: Two paddle faces: one smooth and one textured/gritty.

options.text: Smooth paddle face
Textured/rough paddle face

explanation.correct: Textured faces grip the ball better, creating more spin.
explanation.incorrect: Rough surfaces create spin, not smooth ones.

lessons.title: Watching the finals together
lessons.objective: Follow along with someone watching a match and ask what just happened.

payload.title: Watching the finals
payload.setting: You and Riley are watching a pro match stream.

exchanges.theirMessage: Oh no, look at that third-shot drop. It landed too high.

replies.text: Too high means the other team can attack it, right?
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. See? Boom, smash.
replies.coachNote: You showed you understood the impact of the bad shot.

replies.text: Oh no, bad shot.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, they're going to pay for that.
replies.coachNote: Agreeing is safe but asking why it's bad deepens it.

replies.text: Why are they so bad at this?
replies.theirResponse: They're pro. One bad shot happens.
replies.coachNote: Don't mock pros. One mistake is normal in any game.

exchanges.theirMessage: And we're tied 1-1. Two games each then DreamBreaker.

replies.text: So the next game decides everything? Winner takes all?
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. Huge pressure game.
replies.coachNote: You grasped the stakes correctly.

replies.text: This is intense!
replies.theirResponse: Right? So close.
replies.coachNote: Sharing enthusiasm is good; add understanding next time.

replies.text: So they just play until someone wins?
replies.theirResponse: No, DreamBreaker is a tiebreak game to 21.
replies.coachNote: You didn't quite understand the format. Ask for clarity.

payload.closingNote: Watching together means asking what just happened and why it matters. Show interest in the strategy.

statement.speaker: Taylor
statement.text: Did you see that dink rally? Someone finally popped one up and it was over.

payload.question: What is Taylor describing?

options.text: A long soft rally where one player hit too high, the opponent attacked and won.
A player served and the return went over the net.
A player got lucky and hit a random shot that worked.
A player reset the ball and they started over.

payload.translation: In a dink rally (soft kitchen shots), the first player to hit the ball too high (pop it up) loses the rally. The opponent attacks the pop-up and wins the point.

followUps.line: Understanding dink rallies is key to following pro matches.
followUps.why: Dinking is the core of pickleball.

followUps.line: Ask Taylor who had the better dink placement.
followUps.why: Shows you're following the strategy, not just the result.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Dink rallies are the heart of pickleball. Watch and learn the pattern: patience wins until someone pops it up.

payload.prompt: While watching a pro match, what helps you follow along?

options.text: Asking your person 'what just happened?' and listening to their explanation.
Pretending you understand everything and nodding along silently.
Criticizing the players' shots.
Checking your phone instead of watching.

explanation.correct: Asking honest questions and listening to their expert commentary is the best way to learn and bond.
explanation.incorrect: Pretending, criticizing or ignoring all miss the opportunity to connect.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask what happened. She'll love explaining the play.

payload.prompt: In a dink rally, whoever hits the ball hardest usually wins the point. True?

scene.alt: A long dink rally at the kitchen.

explanation.correct: Dink rallies are won by patience, precision and soft placement, not power.
explanation.incorrect: In dinking, the player who keeps it soft and low wins. Hard hits end dinks badly.
explanation.sayThisLine: Dinking = patience. Whoever pops it up first loses.

lessons.title: Rating talk
lessons.objective: Handle conversations about skill levels and DUPR without fake confidence.

payload.title: Rating talk
payload.setting: Sam is discussing skill progression after open play.

exchanges.theirMessage: I'm a 3.5 but pushing for 4.0. So close.

replies.text: What's the one thing you think would help you break into 4.0?
replies.theirResponse: Consistency on third-shot drops. That's my weak link.
replies.coachNote: Asking about the goal shows interest in her progression.

replies.text: You're probably already a 4.0 in your head.
replies.theirResponse: Nah, I need to earn it.
replies.coachNote: Fake praise backfires. Ask about real progress instead.

replies.text: I could probably beat you.
replies.theirResponse: ...OK then.
replies.coachNote: Never challenge someone's rating. It's not about ego.

exchanges.theirMessage: My DUPR is 3.8, which is better than my self-rating.

replies.text: So the system rated you higher? Does that feel right?
replies.theirResponse: Maybe I'm playing better in tournaments than I thought.
replies.coachNote: You showed you understood DUPR and asked for her take.

replies.text: Cool, that's good.
replies.theirResponse: I think so.
replies.coachNote: Generic. Ask what it means to her.

replies.text: DUPR is just a number. Doesn't matter.
replies.theirResponse: It matters to me for tournament placement.
replies.coachNote: Ratings matter to serious players. Don't dismiss them.

payload.closingNote: Skill ratings are real and meaningful. Ask about progress; never challenge their rating or offer unsolicited advice.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: Everyone in that bracket was sandbagging. These 3.5s were playing 4.0 level.

payload.question: What does Jordan mean?

options.text: Players were rated lower than their actual skill to get a competitive advantage in brackets.
The players were exhausted and playing poorly.
The players were helping each other win.
Nobody understood the rating system.

payload.translation: Sandbagging is when a player rates themselves below their true skill level to compete in an easier bracket and win prizes they shouldn't.

followUps.line: Sandbagging is controversial because it ruins fair competition.
followUps.why: Shows you understand the issue's impact.

followUps.line: Ask if Jordan suspects it was intentional or just how tournaments shake out.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Sandbagging is real and unfair. Acknowledge the frustration without becoming judge.

payload.prompt: When someone says they're a 3.5 trying to reach 4.0, what's the best response?

options.text: Ask what the main challenge is for that jump.
Tell them you're already a 5.0.
Say that ratings don't matter.
Suggest they're probably overrated.

explanation.correct: Asking about the challenge shows interest in their goals and progression.
explanation.incorrect: Bragging, dismissing or doubting all miss the point of the conversation.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask about the next level. That's how you show you care about her growth.

pairs.definition: A player's skill level on a scale from 2.5 to 5.0+; affects tournament bracket placement.
Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating; a system that tracks skill based on match results.
Playing or rating below your true skill level to compete in an easier bracket.

explanation.summary: Rating = skill level; DUPR = match-based rating; sandbagging = unfair undercutting.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ratings are how the sport tracks skill fairly. Respect them.

lessons.title: Her team lost
lessons.objective: Support an MLP fan after a heartbreaking loss without dismissing fandom.

payload.title: Her team lost
payload.setting: Casey's favorite MLP team lost in the DreamBreaker.

exchanges.theirMessage: We lost again. DreamBreaker. I can't even watch the replay.

replies.text: That's brutal. 2-2 then lost in the tiebreak? That hurts.
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. So close and still not enough.
replies.coachNote: You showed you understood the format and the pain.

replies.text: It's just a game.
replies.theirResponse: ...It matters to me.
replies.coachNote: Never minimize someone's fandom. It's real.

replies.text: That team is just not good enough.
replies.theirResponse: They played their hearts out.
replies.coachNote: Don't criticize the team. She's loyal and hurting.

exchanges.theirMessage: We're in playoff position but this loss stings.

replies.text: You're still in. Games left to come back. This doesn't define the season.
replies.theirResponse: I know. But today was our best shot.
replies.coachNote: You reminded her of the bigger picture without dismissing the loss.

replies.text: Yeah.
replies.theirResponse: Not exactly reassuring.
replies.coachNote: One word doesn't cut it. Show you care.

replies.text: Just switch to rooting for the team that's winning.
replies.theirResponse: That's not how loyalty works.
replies.coachNote: Sports fans don't switch. Loyalty is the point.

payload.closingNote: MLP fans are passionate. After a loss, show empathy and remind them the season continues.

statement.speaker: Morgan
statement.text: My team's roster is so strong on paper but they keep losing to weaker squads on the road.

payload.question: What is Morgan talking about?

options.text: The team plays worse away from home despite having good players and strategy.
The roster isn't actually good and Morgan is overestimating them.
The league is rigging results against the team.
There's a problem with the team roster on official documents.

payload.translation: On paper (in theory), the team has strong players, but in actual matches (especially away from home), performance doesn't match expectations.

followUps.line: Home/away performance is a real thing in team sports.
followUps.why: Shows you understand the fan frustration.

followUps.line: Ask if she thinks it's pressure, travel, or something else.
followUps.why: Engages with the analysis she's doing.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Team sports involve travel, pressure and form. Ask what she thinks is behind the pattern.

payload.prompt: After her favorite team loses, what helps most?

options.text: Show empathy, acknowledge the loss hurt, remind her the season continues.
Tell her to stop being so emotionally invested.
Point out the team's weaknesses and why they deserved to lose.
Suggest she root for a better team instead.

explanation.correct: Empathy, validation and perspective help a fan through disappointment.
explanation.incorrect: Dismissing, criticizing or mocking all drive people away.
explanation.sayThisLine: Empathy first. Remind her the season has more games. That's it.

payload.prompt: Your person just texted that their MLP team lost and they're devastated. What do you do?

situation.narrative: She's passionate about her team. A loss hurts.

facts.label: What she said
facts.value: We just lost a crucial playoff-positioning game.

options.label: Reach out and ask what happened; listen
options.consequence: Perfect. You show you care and create space for her to process.

options.label: Ignore it and change the subject later
options.consequence: She'll feel unsupported and alone in her disappointment.
considerations: You miss a moment to connect

payload.expertNote: MLP fans live and die with their teams. A supportive text means everything after a tough loss.

lessons.title: "You should come play"
lessons.objective: Accept an invitation to play honestly, admitting what you don't know.

payload.title: Come play with us
payload.setting: Riley invites you to open play for the first time.

exchanges.theirMessage: We need a fourth this Saturday. Come play with us!

replies.text: I'd love to! Fair warning: total beginner. Can I borrow a paddle?
replies.theirResponse: Perfect. You'll be fine. I'll show you the kitchen.
replies.coachNote: Honest about your level puts her at ease and you both relax.

replies.text: I'm not sure I'm good enough.
replies.theirResponse: Nobody's perfect. Just come.
replies.coachNote: Humble but maybe overthinking. Say yes and be honest about level.

replies.text: Sure, I'm basically a 4.0 already.
replies.theirResponse: Uh... we'll see about that.
replies.coachNote: Faking a level backfires in the first rally. Honesty wins.

exchanges.theirMessage: It's super chill, just open play. Everyone helps out.

replies.text: I trust you. What should I bring besides a sense of humor?
replies.theirResponse: Court shoes if you have them, water, that's it. Bring the humor.
replies.coachNote: You showed confidence in her guidance and added warmth.

replies.text: Oh good, that makes me feel better.
replies.theirResponse: You're going to have fun.
replies.coachNote: It's genuine but doesn't add much. Ask a practical question.

replies.text: So nobody cares if I'm bad? That's weak.
replies.theirResponse: ...Everyone cares a little. Just be a good sport.
replies.coachNote: Calling the sport or community 'weak' is insulting.

payload.closingNote: Being honest about your level is braver and kinder than faking. Say yes, ask what to bring, and show up with curiosity.

payload.prompt: You're invited to play but worried you'll embarrass yourself. What do you say?

situation.narrative: She wants you to join. You're nervous.

facts.label: What you feel
facts.value: Anxious about being the worst player.

options.label: Say yes, be honest about nerves, ask what to expect
options.consequence: Honest acceptance with real questions builds connection and sets expectations.

options.label: Say yes and pretend you're experienced
options.consequence: She'll notice immediately during play and feel misled.

payload.expertNote: Honesty about level is attractive. Faking it is the opposite.

statement.speaker: Devon
statement.text: I'm still learning the kitchen rule. It's confusing.

payload.question: What is Devon doing?

options.text: Being honest about not understanding a core rule and open to learning.
Admitting they're a bad player and will never improve.
Pretending to learn to impress someone.
Saying they're giving up on pickleball.

payload.translation: Saying 'I'm still learning' or 'I don't understand' is strength, not weakness. It opens the door to genuine connection.

followUps.line: Admitting gaps is smarter than faking expertise.
Ask her to explain the kitchen rule so you both get clarity.
followUps.why: Turns confusion into a learning moment together.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Saying 'I'm still learning' builds trust. Pretending you know when you don't destroys it.

payload.prompt: When you don't understand a pickleball concept, what's the best move?

options.text: Say 'I'm still learning that' and ask them to explain.
Nod and pretend you understand.
Change the subject so she doesn't know you're lost.
Tell her she's explaining it wrong.

explanation.correct: Admitting gaps and asking for help is honest and invites her to teach you.
explanation.incorrect: Pretending, dodging or blaming all erode trust.
explanation.sayThisLine: Honesty beats fake knowledge every time.

lessons.title: Say-this gauntlet
lessons.objective: Decode five real fan/player lines in quick succession.

statement.speaker: Five quick lines
statement.text: Five real things pickleball fans say. Decode each one.

payload.question: What does each line mean?

options.text: "I got pickled last night." = Lost 11-0 (shutout).
options.explanation: Pickled is a shutout loss. A tough pill to swallow.

options.text: "My dink game is off today." = Soft kitchen shots aren't landing low.
options.explanation: Off dinking = losing control of soft shots near the net.

options.text: "They called it out but it was on the line." = A disputed line call.
options.explanation: Line calls are subjective. This is a common frustration.

options.text: "I'm a 3.5 but playing like a 2.5 today." = Off day, not to skill.
options.explanation: Rating vs performance. Everyone has off days.

options.text: "Let's stack for this game." = Partners stay on same side for a rally.
options.explanation: Stacking is a tactical choice to keep strengths in place.

payload.translation: These five lines are what you'll hear at courts and streams. You now recognize all of them.

followUps.line: You've seen all the core terminology now.
followUps.why: You can follow conversations and ask smart follow-ups.

followUps.line: Use these lines in conversation to show you understand.
followUps.why: Hearing them from you feels natural to her.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You don't need to use all these terms yourself, just understand them when she does.

payload.prompt: After hearing any of these lines, what's your reflex move?

options.text: Ask a curious follow-up that shows you understood the line.
Change the subject.
Offer unsolicited advice about what they should do.
Repeat the line back as if you said it.

explanation.correct: A follow-up question shows you got it and care about the story.
explanation.incorrect: Dodging, advising or faking all kill the conversation flow.
explanation.sayThisLine: Understand the line, ask a follow-up. That's how you're now part of the conversation.

payload.prompt: If someone says "I'm a 3.5," they're giving you a real metric of their skill level. True?

choices.label: True, it's a real skill measure

explanation.correct: Ratings are real benchmarks. A 3.5 has specific strengths and gaps vs 4.0.
explanation.incorrect: Ratings matter. They define tournament brackets and competitive levels.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rating = skill. Respect it. It matters to them.

pairs.definition: Soft kitchen shot; the foundation of pickleball.
Whether the ball is in or out; self-officiated in open play.

distractorDefinitions: An ancient name for the game

explanation.summary: Dink = soft shot; pickled = shutout; line call = boundary judgment.
explanation.sayThisLine: You now understand the core conversation vocabulary. You're in.
